components.text: Whether the narrated conversion and beneficial transformation provide distinctive support for Christianity rather than a direction-neutral conversion pattern.
Whether Bignon's conversion experience supplies evidential support for Christianity rather than merely reporting a personally transformative sequence.
Whether Bignon relies merely on conversion testimony or on particular coordinated events whose likelihood differs between Christianity and atheism.
Whether Bignon's case depends merely on the existence of a conversion narrative and is therefore neutralized by reverse-conversion stories.
Whether the allegedly improbable coordinated events are less expected under naturalism once population size, familiar scripts, and ordinary coincidence are considered.
Whether the cited pattern of coincidences is genuinely less expected under naturalism than under a Christian providential hypothesis.
Whether the aggregate comparative arguments rationally compel a uniquely Christian conclusion rather than permit continued reasonable disagreement.
Whether the debate should require the experiential case to compel a unique verdict or instead assess whether belief remains rationally permissible.
Whether failure to compel atheists defeats the more modest claim that Christian belief can be rationally permissible and personally justified.
Whether failure to compel atheists defeats the claim that Bignon's conversion can be intellectually sensible and personally justified.
Whether the naturalistic coincidence account must be disproved before Bignon can claim a personally rational interpretation.
Whether sustained expert inquiry produces convergence sufficient to raise the case beyond rational permissibility to compelling public support.
Whether rationally serious inquiry should be expected to compel convergence beyond the modest standard of personal permissibility.
Whether a modest cumulative Christian case must also reckon with a structurally parallel naturalist case and major counterarguments from evil and hiddenness.
Whether providential interpretation remains comparatively adequate after arguments from evil and divine hiddenness are included.
Whether a cumulative Christian case can claim rational support without also confronting a structurally parallel naturalist case and major contrary arguments.
Whether selective providential action is compatible with the evidential force of evil and divine hiddenness.
Whether selective providential intervention is inconsistent with God's not converting everyone or can be compatible with morally sufficient reasons.
Whether providential guidance of Bignon is inconsistent with uneven conversion, persistent nonbelief, and the hiddenness-related challenge.
Whether selective providence can explain the culturally and historically uneven content of reported religious experiences without weakening Christian specificity.
Whether interpretation of personally salient experience remains distinctively Christian once cultural dependence is considered.
Whether religious experience can specifically justify Christian interpretation once culturally and historically divergent experiences are considered.
Whether uneven religious interpretation is adequately explained by selective providence or instead reflects cultural dependence.
Whether diverse non-Christian experiences uniformly defeat Christianity or can instead count against naturalism while requiring case-specific theological assessment.
Whether non-Christian and culturally diverse religious experiences neutralize Bignon's Christian experience or can be assessed differentially.
Whether all directionally opposed experiences possess equal evidential status merely because they are reported.
Whether preferring Christianity amid diverse incompatible experiences is arbitrary special pleading or justified by stronger comparative reasons.
Whether preferring the Christian interpretation amid diverse religious claims is arbitrary special pleading or rests on comparative reasons.
How incompatible but apparently comparable Christian and Muslim experiences can be adjudicated without simply privileging one's own experience.
How incompatible but phenomenologically comparable Christian and Muslim experiences can be adjudicated without arbitrary preference.
Whether historical and intellectual evidence can supply discrimination even when experience alone does not compel convergence.
Whether comparative historical evidence plainly favors Christianity over Islam strongly enough to adjudicate an experiential tie.
Whether comparative historical evidence plainly breaks the experiential tie in Christianity's favor.
Whether the claimed better reasons for Christianity have been established through competent comparative assessment.
Whether Christianity can claim a comparative historical advantage based on source quality, quantity, and tested reliability rather than mere confidence.
Whether Christianity lacks a clear comparative historical advantage over Islam once source quality and reliability are considered.
Whether the larger quantity of Christian documents independently indicates historical superiority or partly reflects later preservation and institutional selection.
Whether the greater quantity of surviving Christian documents independently demonstrates superior historical support.
Whether source quality and claim-specific reliability, apart from quantity, establish Christian superiority.
